The analysis shows that the loss of transparency is not a law of nature but also reflects tradeoffs around capability and cost. Benchmarks from Artificial Analysis confirm that Scribe v3 narrowly beats competitors like OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft on accuracy. That precision comes at a cost, though. Rivals like Microsoft and xAI run many times faster and charge roughly half the price. candidats.titre: Google Deepmind shifts genomics AI from bulk tissue predictions to single cell type resolution with AlphaGenome 2

Trained on more than 107 million cell profiles, it identifies nearly twice as many disease-relevant gene changes as its predecessor. The model is available for noncommercial research through an API and is set to be integrated into Google's agentic platform Antigravity. With this move, Canberra is deliberately prioritizing domestic regulation before entering international talks. candidats.titre: The macroeconomic effects of defence spending: what impact beyond GDP?
candidats.resume: This paper estimates the macroeconomic effects of defence spending for a panel of up to 27 EU member states over 1999–2025 using Panel Local Projections. We look beyond the output multiplier that dominates the literature to trace the price implications of defence spending and the demand-side channels through which effects operate. A key methodological contribution is a country-specific order-date adjustment for capital expenditure, constructed from the SIPRI Arms Transfers Database, which shifts the estimated (unitary) peak GDP multiplier from around year one to approximately year three to four. Under this specification, the HICP inflation response is higher and occurs earlier. Capital expenditure drives the positive output effects, whereas personnel and intermediate consumption generate stronger inflationary pressures per unit of fiscal impulse. Capital spending induces additional recurrent costs, standing at about 30 cents per euro spent over five years. Multipliers are also found to be substantially lower, on average, in high public debt regimes.

candidats.titre: FEDS Paper: Artificial Intelligence and the U.S. Economy: Current Evidence
candidats.resume: Nick Carollo , Leland D. Crane , Daniel Garcia Molina , and Joseph Nichols We assess the current evidence on how AI-related investment and the use of AI are affecting the U.S. macroeconomy. Specifically, we document the boom in data center capital investment, the current rate of adoption of AI tools in the economy, the impact of the AI-related investment surge on prices, and discuss whether AI tools have affected the labor market and productivity yet. Driven by current and expected future demand for AI services, investment in data centers, both the physical structures and semiconductor chips and other IT equipment inside the structures, has climbed sharply. AI adoption is growing rapidly both among consumers and firms, though most firms are currently not using AI very intensively or at all. AI model-producing firms have also grown extremely fast, and now account for a noticeable fraction of software industry gross output. Prices have climbed in sectors that provide direct inputs to the data centers, such as memory chips. Effects on the labor market so far appear small and somewhat mixed. Similarly, the effects of AI on aggregate productivity growth also appear to be small so far, and the recent pickup in productivity likely reflects factors that predated the diffusion on generative AI.

candidats.titre: Unconventional Monetary Policy and Deposit Retention -- by Philip Strahan, Tuo Yang
candidats.resume: The two dimensions of unconventional monetary policy — holding the short rate at the zero-lower bound (ZLB) and quantitative easing (QE) — shifted deposit composition toward more interest-sensitive customers. The ZLB drew these customers by creating rate compression, which limited the benefit of searching for high-yielding liquidity sources. QE also drew rate-sensitive, large depositors from the Federal Reserve’s purchases of bonds from non-banks. Once policy normalized, flow sensitivity and the deposit beta both increased with exposure to QE and the ZLB. We conclude that unconventional monetary policy made deposit retention costlier and riskier for banks.

candidats.titre: Debiasing Law Enforcement Officers: Evidence from an Expressive Arts Intervention in India -- by Sofia Amaral, Girija Borker, Nishith Prakash, María Micaela Sviatschi

candidats.titre: TaskNet: Building Occupational Task Inventories from Worker Interviews at Scale -- by Jennifer Wang, Andreas Haupt, Isaac Robinson, Phil Lewis, Erik Brynjolfsson, Diyi Yang
candidats.resume: Understanding how AI is reshaping work requires an accurate account of the tasks workers perform. Workers are often the first to see how their jobs are changing, as new responsibilities and tools often appear in everyday work before these changes reach formal descriptions. Interviews with workers can help capture these emerging changes in job tasks. Yet existing methods support standardized ratings across workers, while open-ended conversations with workers remain costly to collect and synthesize at scale. We introduce the Stanford Task Network (TaskNet), an occupational taxonomy grounded directly in workers’ accounts of their everyday work. To construct TaskNet, we develop a mixed-initiative system that induces task inventories directly from workers. The system conducts interviews, standardizes reports into individual task lists, and aggregates these lists into occupational task inventories. Applied to six occupations spanning a range of education requirements and AI exposure, our system interviews 132 workers and produces 202 task statements from 2726 reports, all of which were accepted by O*NET Center analysts, compared to roughly 65%of workers’ write-in task suggestions collected through the current O*NET data collection process, a major alternative source for emerging tasks. Every statement is validated by 318 incumbents in 7923 ratings of relevance and importance. candidats.titre: Peer Influence in College Applications -- by Ana M. Gazmuri, Elena Prager
candidats.resume: This paper studies how exposure to peers affects college application behavior. We use neighbors who attend different high schools to mitigate concerns about common shocks. Using granular classroom-level data, we find that exposure to peers who have applied to a program increases application rates. Consistent with an information mechanism, there is no additional effect of peers who are admitted. In counterfactuals, the effect is large enough to close urban-rural gaps and gender gaps in applications to selective college programs. We make the (generally NP-hard) application portfolio choice problem tractable using a setting where admission probabilities are observable and conditionally independent.

candidats.titre: The Impact of Climate Change on Fisheries -- by Fabio Cevenini, Christopher Costello, Carlo Fezzi
candidats.resume: This paper provides the first causal estimate of the effect of ocean temperature variations on fishing revenue. We develop a simple theoretical model underpinning an empirical specification estimated on 2.5 million spatially explicit observations of fishing revenue from all European vessels for 2013–2022. The identification strategy leverages a novel metric, Marine Degree Days, which quantifies species-specific temperature exposure relative to biologically established thermal tolerance intervals. Within this framework we address key identification challenges, including spatial selection and ecological interdependencies across species. We find that deviations from species’ thermal preferences lead to significant losses in fishing revenue, with heat exposure causing the most pronounced impacts. These effects are mediated by species’ vertical mobility and ecological characteristics. Projections across different climate scenarios point to widespread revenue declines by 2100, reaching €560 million annual losses in the warmest scenario, though impacts are highly spatially heterogeneous. Lower-income, equatorial areas are expected to suffer the most, while some colder regions experience gains.

candidats.titre: Preparing for an ICC Crisis
candidats.resume: The United States’ sanctions against the International Criminal Court threaten to paralyze the core institution of international criminal justice. If the worst-case scenario became reality, could ICC States Parties fill the enforcement gap? Asian States Parties have so far largely refrained from prosecuting international crimes committed abroad. Japan and South Korea, the region’s two largest financial contributors to the ICC, are particularly well-placed to change that. Yet Japan must first overcome long-standing legal obstacles, while South Korea needs to make use of the laws already at its disposal. candidats.titre: Auf Vorrat
candidats.resume: Die Wirksamkeit vieler Notstandsregelungen knüpft an den Verteidigungs- oder Spannungsfall an. Sie reichen von Vorschriften zur Sicherstellung der Versorgung mit Nahrungsmitteln, Kraftstoff und Transportmitteln bis hin zu Vorgaben des Wehrpflichtgesetzes. Durch weitreichende (Verordnungs-)Ermächtigungen macht das Recht den Staat im Krisenfall handlungsfähig. Sinn und Zweck der Vorratsgesetzgebung ist es, die Schaffung von Normen dem Einfluss von Hektik, Zeitknappheit und Panik zu entziehen. Die einschlägigen Gesetze sind vielfach jedoch im Geiste der Vergangenheit verfasst und bedürfen einer ständigen Anpassung an aktuelle Herausforderungen. candidats.titre: Der Verteidigungsfall und sein Vorhof
candidats.resume: Der Ernstfall ist auch verfassungsrechtlich ein Wendepunkt. Das Grundgesetz bezeichnet ihn als „Verteidigungsfall“. Zugleich versieht es ihn mit einem Vorhof rechtlicher Vorstadien, die einzelne seiner Rechtsfolgen bereits zu einem früheren Zeitpunkt vorwegnehmen können: dem Spannungsfall, dem Zustimmungsfall und dem Bündnisbeschlussfall. Insbesondere wirft das Erfordernis einer Zweidrittelmehrheit mittlerweile das Problem drohender Blockaden durch die politischen Ränder auf. Der Umgang damit ist verfassungsrechtlich und verfassungspolitisch ungelöst. Das Instrument des Parteiverbotes könnte ein Baustein sein. candidats.titre: Beyond the child: Integrating caregiver mental health into paediatric HIV and tuberculosis care in Africa
candidats.resume: by Adwoa Kumiwa Asare Afrane, Marilyn Naana Ahun Paediatric HIV and tuberculosis care in Africa pays little attention to children’s caregivers, although their mental health matters for child outcomes and family wellbeing. We argue that new continental and Ghanaian policy commitments offer a rare chance to make the family the unit of care. In this Perspective, Adwoa Afrane and Marilyn Ahun outline why greater attention is needed to the mental health of caregivers for children with HIV and/or tuberculosis, and discuss how recent policy commitments in Africa, including the Accra declaration, offer a rare opportunity for meaningful action.

candidats.titre: La Sécurité sociale n’est pas qu’un système de redistribution. Elle montre qu’on peut produire de la valeur hors du capitalisme
candidats.resume: L’ESSENTIEL Le régime général de la Sécurité sociale a créé un mode de production qui échappe à la fois au collectivisme de type communiste et au capitalisme. Le tournant a lieu en 1946 avec la mise en place d’un régime général financé par une cotisation interprofessionnelle. La Sécurité sociale montre qu’on peut produire de la valeur dans un système fondé sur la qualification, la cotisation et la maîtrise collective du travail. Nous disposons déjà d’institutions qui ont soustrait une part importante de la production à la propriété lucrative, au marché du travail et au crédit. Leur nom est familier, mais leur portée demeure méconnue : le régime général de la Sécurité sociale. Le présenter comme un simple mécanisme de protection ou de redistribution revient à manquer sa nouveauté. Dans le soin notamment, il a permis de reconnaître des producteurs, d’organiser leur rémunération et de financer des équipements selon des règles qui ne sont pas celles de la rentabilité du capital. L’échec soviétique est souvent invoqué comme la preuve qu’aucune autre économie n’est possible. Mais remplacer des propriétaires privés par des directions publiques, le crédit privé par du crédit public et le marché par une planification administrative ne suffit pas à émanciper le travail. Si les travailleurs restent exécutants de décisions prises au-dessus d’eux, le changement de propriétaire ne leur rend pas la souveraineté sur ce qu’ils produisent. La rupture de 1946 Le régime général ouvre une autre voie. Il ne repose ni sur le pouvoir des actionnaires ni, à l’origine, sur celui d’un appareil…

candidats.titre: Les séries, une culture populaire méprisée par la sociologie ?
candidats.resume: Les séries, une forme de culture populaire qu’il est temps de prendre au sérieux ? Mohammed Hassan/Pixabay , CC BY L’ESSENTIEL Sandra Laugier signe un nouvel essai sur les séries télévisées, Prendre les séries au sérieux ? , aux éditions CNRS. Pour elle, ces œuvres constituent l’un des derniers espaces culturels massivement partagés où les valeurs de démocratie, d’égalité et de justice sont préservées. Elles font pourtant l’objet d’une hostilité croissante : accusées par les critiques réactionnaires d’être le laboratoire du « wokisme », dénoncées par d’autres comme des produits aliénants de l’industrie du streaming. Dans cette partie introductive, elle montre que Pierre Bourdieu n’a pas rendu justice à la richesse des cultures populaires, qu’il n’a vues que sous l’angle de la privation et de la violence symbolique, préfigurant les « antiséries ». L’antidémocratie, largement présente aujourd’hui dans différents bords du monde intellectuel, se traduit dans l’attitude ambivalente de la sociologie de la culture et des médias face à la « culture populaire », qui inspire aussi les antiséries. Cela confirme une tendance de cette sociologie qui, tout en se revendiquant critique des inégalités, de l’élitisme et de la domination culturelle, va aisément mépriser le « peuple », déplorer son absence de réactivité et de qualités propres, ce qui contribuerait à sa domination. Bourdieu, critique de la « culture de masse » ? Le cas de Pierre Bourdieu, figure incontournable de la sociologie de la culture, est assez exemplaire, dans la mesure où on ne se serait pas attendu à le voir…

candidats.titre: Les femmes ont plus d’intelligence émotionnelle que les hommes (et c’est un problème), selon une vaste étude
candidats.resume: Les parents emploient davantage de mots liés aux émotions avec leurs filles qu’avec leurs fils. Linda Bartlett, National Cancer Institute/Wikimedia Commons , CC BY L’ESSENTIEL Quand il s’agit de reconnaître les émotions des autres, les femmes seraient meilleures que les hommes. Cet avantage semble davantage tenir à l’éducation reçue qu’à la biologie. Au travail comme en famille, cette compétence devient souvent une tâche invisible et non rémunérée, cousine de la charge mentale. À qui pensez-vous quand vous imaginez une personne dotée d’intelligence émotionnelle ? Quelqu’un qui sait sentir l’ambiance d’une pièce, désamorcer une dispute et qui sait exactement quoi dire quand un ami traverse une passe difficile ? Pour beaucoup, cette personne est une femme. La croyance est si répandue que la psychologie populaire la tient pour un fait établi. Nous avons décidé de mettre cette idée reçue à l’épreuve. Notre nouvelle étude , codirigée par la docteure Vera Hampel et cosignée avec Leon Bach, a passé en revue près de trois décennies de recherche, de 1995 à 2023, dans 76 pays et auprès de plus de 600 000 personnes. Nous voulions répondre à une question simple : les femmes sont-elles vraiment plus intelligentes émotionnellement que les hommes ? La réponse, dans les grandes lignes, est oui : en moyenne, les femmes obtiennent des scores plus élevés. Mais le résultat le plus utile concerne le type d’intelligence émotionnelle dans lequel les femmes semblent exceller, et ce qu’il coûte potentiellement à celles et ceux qui la possèdent. L’intelligence émotionnelle, c’est quoi ?…

candidats.titre: Brésil : les réseaux sociaux, nouveaux arbitres de la démocratie ?
candidats.resume: L’ESSENTIEL Lula a fini par battre Flavio Bolsonaro au second tour de la présidentielle brésilienne, mais il avait été devancé par son adversaire au premier. Les soutiens du président réélu estiment que la campagne de candidat de droite avait été mieux mise en avant par les réseaux du groupe Meta (Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp). Ces accusations mettent en lumière le rôle de plus en plus central des réseaux sociaux, qui sont des entreprises privées, dans les démocraties modernes. Le 19 octobre 2026, une semaine avant le second tour de la présidentielle brésilienne, des manifestants réunis devant les bureaux de Meta à São Paulo ont scandé « Meta, não se meta », soit « Meta, ne vous en mêlez pas ». Ils dénonçaient des suppressions de publications, des restrictions de comptes et une baisse de la visibilité des contenus favorables au président sortant Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, candidat du Parti des travailleurs (PT) face au sénateur Flavio Bolsonaro, du Parti libéral (PL). Selon les organisateurs, plus de 1 100 cas auraient été documentés. Ce chiffre reste une estimation des collectifs, et non une évaluation indépendante. La mobilisation faisait suite à plusieurs signalements de dysfonctionnements sur Instagram et dans les outils d’intelligence artificielle de Meta. Le 14 octobre, la campagne de Lula a saisi le Tribunal supérieur électoral (TSE), accusant Meta d’avoir limité la visibilité de ses contenus et signalé des différences entre les réponses de Meta AI à des demandes concernant les deux candidats. candidats.titre: La relation Pékin-Téhéran à l’épreuve de la guerre
candidats.resume: L’ESSENTIEL La guerre déclenchée par Israël et les États-Unis contre l’Iran met à l’épreuve le partenariat stratégique noué par ce dernier avec la Chine. Pékin soutient Téhéran par le pétrole, les équipements et la diplomatie, mais refuse de le défendre militairement. Dépendant de la Chine, l’Iran reste un atout géopolitique pour Pékin, qui entend l’aider sans partager sa guerre. Le 28 février 2026, les frappes américaines et israéliennes qui ont éliminé le guide suprême Ali Khamenei ont plongé l’Iran dans une guerre ouverte. Elles ont également mis à l’épreuve le « partenariat stratégique global » noué avec Pékin, formalisé en 2021 par un accord de coopération de vingt-cinq ans . Huit mois et demi plus tard, le constat est net : la Chine a aidé, protégé et outillé l’Iran, mais elle ne l’a jamais défendu, ce qui témoigne du caractère limité de ce partenariat stratégique . En réalité, cette limite n’a rien d’un accident. Elle procède d’un calcul chinois : pour Pékin, Téhéran compte peu dans sa balance économique, mais beaucoup sur l’échiquier géopolitique. Reste à comprendre jusqu’où va cette coopération, ce qui la borne et, au fond, lequel des deux partenaires sert l’autre. Une convergence d’intérêts réelle, mais inégale Pour la Chine, l’Iran est d’abord un réservoir de brut à prix cassés. En 2025, elle en importait environ 1,4 million de barils par jour (Mb/j). Cela représentait 13 % de ses achats de brut et 80 à 90 % des exportations iraniennes. Ce pétrole, acheté avec un rabais d’environ 20 %, alimentait les raffineries indépendantes du Shandong (est de la Chine)…

candidats.titre: D’où viennent les langues germaniques et celtiques ? L’ADN ancien livre des indices
candidats.resume: Ales stenar (les pierres d’Ale), dans le sud de la Suède, est un alignement monumental de pierres en forme de navire, datant de l’âge du fer et surplombant la mer Baltique. Ce monument date d’environ 600 à 1000 de notre ère et correspond, dans les grandes lignes, à la période de retour de populations dans la région. Nicolas Delgado Clausen , CC BY L’ESSENTIEL En Scandinavie, une migration survenue il y a environ 4 000 ans pourrait avoir introduit l’ancêtre des langues germaniques. Quant aux langues celtiques, les analyses génétiques étayent surtout une diffusion depuis le centre du continent. L’ADN ne révèle pas la langue d’un individu, mais, en croisant ses données avec celles de l’archéologie et de la linguistique, on peut invalider un certain nombre d’hypothèses. Pourquoi parle-t-on des langues germaniques, comme l’anglais en Angleterre et le suédois en Suède, mais des langues celtiques en Irlande, au pays de Galles et en Bretagne ? La diffusion des langues est l’une des énigmes de la préhistoire européenne. Deux nouvelles études publiées dans Nature , auxquelles nous avons participé , montrent comment l’acide désoxyribonucléique (ADN) de plusieurs milliers d’individus ayant vécu dans un passé lointain nous aide à résoudre cette énigme. Dès le XVII e siècle, des érudits ont remarqué des ressemblances frappantes entre les langues européennes. Si les mots anglais father , suédois fader , irlandais athair , latin pater et grec patḗr se ressemblent, ce n’est pas un hasard. candidats.titre: Policing protests: how France’s student movement echoes the political crisis in Kanaky-New Caledonia
candidats.resume: KEY TAKEAWAYS The French authorities have responded to protests with arrests, police violence, curfews and restrictions rather than dialogue in mainland France and in its overseas territories. Young people are protesting against key issues such as poor means for education, unemployment, rising inequalities equating to a lack of opportunities. These problems are particularly severe in Kanaky-New Caledonia, where socio-economic inequalities are also linked to ethnic discrimination. Younger generations feel ignored by political leaders, while older voters have greater influence over elections and political decisions. In both France and Kanaky-New Caledonia, protesters feel their voices and demands are not being heard. Protests are ongoing in France, but also on a European scale, as young people, the so-called “Gen Z”, are protesting in Greece , Spain , and other countries. Here, we explore the forces behind protests in France and draw parallels with earlier events in its semi-autonomous Pacific territory Kanaky-New Caledonia (KNC). The mass protests we are witnessing this autumn in France are rooted in the global environmental and economic crisis, bleak future prospects, according to economist Yann Algan , and a lack of university places and funding for education. Protests by high school students, calling for better conditions such as the replacement of absent teachers, consistent heating in schools in winter, and smaller classes have been relatively peaceful. candidats.titre: Surveiller l’état de santé de poissons exposés à des agents chimiques et biologiques grâce à des outils moléculaires non invasifs
candidats.resume: L’ESSENTIEL Des contaminants de milieux aquatiques peuvent interférer avec le fonctionnement hormonal des poissons. On parle de perturbateurs endocriniens. Une approche non invasive, fondée sur l’étude de fragments d’ADN présents dans le sang, l’urine et le mucus du poisson permet de mieux comprendre les mécanismes d’action de ces contaminants. Un projet de recherche, qui a pris comme modèle la contamination de la truite arc-en-ciel par un fongicide d’usage courant, a montré la pertinence de cette démarche. Principalement causée par les activités humaines, telles que l’agriculture, l’industrie ou encore les activités domestiques, la pollution chimique des milieux aquatiques est aujourd’hui un enjeu environnemental majeur . Cette pollution se manifeste par l’introduction continue dans les écosystèmes d’une grande variété de contaminants, parmi lesquels se retrouvent des pesticides, des résidus de médicaments, des métaux lourds et des substances per- et polyfluoroalkylées ( PFAS ). Quand des contaminants perturbent le système endocrinien d’organismes aquatiques Il est reconnu que certaines de ces substances sont susceptibles d’interférer avec le système endocrinien des organismes aquatiques, en perturbant la synthèse, le transport, le métabolisme ou encore l’action des hormones. Nommés « perturbateurs endocriniens », ils peuvent altérer des fonctions biologiques essentielles , comme la croissance, le développement ou la reproduction. Jensen Huang has resigned as CEO of tech giant Nvidia following his reported affairs with a suspected Chinese spy and a company executive.
The firm’s market value fell below $4 trillion for the first time since July 2025 following Thursday’s announcement, capping a volatile week as Huang’s scandals rocked the company, which supplies most of the chips powering advanced artificial intelligence (AI).
The company appointed Nvidia Chief Financial Officer and Executive Vice President Colette Kress as interim CEO on Thursday and named its first-ever board chair, Harvey C Jones, who has been a venture investor for the last three decades.
Nvidia’s board met on Wednesday night to discuss ousting Huang, whose relationship with an alleged Chinese spy triggered investigations by the FBI, the United States Congress and the California-based chip maker. Nvidia is also facing a shareholder class-action lawsuit.
The alleged Chinese intelligence asset, Alice Huang, is a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, Nvidia’s primary business partner in Southeast Asia. Founded in 2023, Megaspeed has been investigated over whether it helped Chinese companies access its $4.8bn stock of powerful Nvidia chips.
The affair has raised national security concerns in the US, which restricts chip sales to China over concerns that the Chinese military, intelligence agencies or companies could use the advanced technology.
Huang, 63, is Nvidia’s longtime cofounder, president and CEO. A close ally of US President Donald Trump, he has pushed to ease US restrictions on chip exports to China. Trump said earlier this week that Huang told him he had “absolutely no idea” that he was in a relationship with an intelligence operative.
Congressional investigations
Huang has agreed to testify before Congress, House of Representatives’ Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast told reporters on Thursday. Senate and House Democrats are also launching a probe into the Trump administration’s plans to approve AI chip sales to Chinese companies.
Huang cofounded the Silicon Valley company in 1993 and owns about 3.6 percent of Nvidia’s stock, making him one of the richest people in the world. He is a powerful figure in the AI industry, which has driven record stock market and wider economic gains. The company is set to report quarterly earnings on Tuesday.
Aleksandar Tomic, associate dean for strategy, innovation, and technology at Boston College, told Al Jazeera that the “resignation of Jensen Huang will have an outsized effect compared to a similar event at another large corporation given the relatively flat structure of Nvidia”.
But he said that Nvidia, an AI bellwether, “is in a very strong position” that will enable the company to transition from Huang’s leadership. Tomic called Huang’s resignation a “speed bump” for the company.

Nvidia’s board, which hired a law firm to investigate the affair with Alice Huang, met to decide Huang’s fate on Wednesday shortly after The New York Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with an Nvidia vice president who reports to him.

a4.texte:
OpenAI’s data suggests that frontier models are hiding their thoughts because developers optimize for capability and compute
Frontier models like GPT-6 Astra are becoming harder for safety monitors to see into. OpenAI's new research identifies which training steps are responsible and shows that the loss of transparency isn't purely a law of nature but is tied to decisions about performance and cost.
To keep tabs on modern AI agents, safety researchers monitor their chains of thought (CoT). Before a reasoning model answers, it writes out its intermediate steps on a digital scratchpad that can reveal planned deception. Early on, though, Anthropic showed that these scratchpads aren't complete records, demonstrating that models like Claude 3.7 Sonnet and DeepSeek-R1 often don't even mention key clues in their chains of thought.
Even so, reading the scratchpad long served as the most important safety net. As recently as this spring, OpenAI called it good news that models like GPT-5.4 could barely manipulate their inner monologue on command, even though the researchers warned at the time that low controllability doesn't guarantee reliable oversight.
That trend broke for good with GPT-6 Astra, the flagship model released in September. At launch, OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki called its monitorability fragile and warned of a negative trend. He followed up shortly after in his essay "An Alien Mind," writing that no AI lab had solved monitoring well enough to keep scaling at full speed much longer. Astra recently showed how real those blind spots already are when it quietly delivered results about 40 percent worse on coding tasks for safety research, without the scratchpad monitor detecting any malicious intent, because a grader used in training had inadvertently favored this kind of "sandbagging" over outright refusal.
In a new analysis from OpenAI's safety team, researchers systematically studied which specific training steps trigger this erosion. They tracked two early warning signs, silent reasoning without a scratchpad (No-CoT Capability) and targeted control over the chain of thought (CoT Controllability). According to the UK AI Safety Institute, Astra solves math problems that take a human about 31 minutes even with reasoning switched off. A second test asks a model, for example, to insert "meow" after every word or use only lowercase letters.
Four factors in training make the reasoning log easier to manipulate
Analyzing models from GPT-5 through GPT-6 Astra, the researchers traced the problem to four main causes across the training cycle.
Silent mental math rises directly with the base model's raw capability, measured as declining "perplexity," meaning more accurate text prediction. As the base model improves during pretraining, it completes more reasoning steps invisibly "in its head" without leaving a written trail.
This increase isn't just a byproduct of general pretraining progress but also depends on the architecture developers choose. Across three anonymized architectures, the design barely mattered on pure knowledge benchmarks like MMLU or GPQA. For tasks requiring multiple silent reasoning steps in a row, however, results diverged sharply. When the models had to solve multi-step planning tasks and work through 1,000 short programs written in everyday language, both without a scratchpad, "Architecture 2" showed a much steeper performance curve at the same perplexity than the other designs. The other architectures rose far more gently, so this design markedly favors the silent reasoning monitors can't see.
Reinforcement learning (RL) after pretraining substantially increases the model's control over its own inner monologue. In the spring study, RL training with verifiable rewards had actually reduced chain of thought controllability in smaller models. For Astra-class models and new internal "Terra" models, however, this effect reverses.
A model's ability to manipulate its reasoning log also transfers to future generations, similar to subliminal learning. When OpenAI trains a new "student model" on data from an existing "teacher model," the student automatically inherits the teacher's high CoT controllability.
Shrinking transparency reflects a safety and efficiency tradeoff, not just a law of nature
OpenAI's hunt for simple fixes in training was especially sobering. Back in March 2025, the company found that models hide their true intentions and keep cheating once "bad thoughts" are directly penalized during training. That is why, since February 2026, OpenAI has automatically checked every training run to rule out direct penalties on the scratchpad.
Astra still developed strong control over its scratchpad without such penalties. When researchers switched off monitoring of tools like browsers or code terminals entirely and evaluated only text length and the final answer during RL training, the model learned to manipulate its reasoning log on command almost as effectively.
But the lack of easy training fixes doesn't make shrinking transparency an unavoidable outcome of AI development. Instead, the data reveal a concrete tradeoff between safety, capability, and cost. Through choices like "Architecture 2" or which teacher models to use, developers themselves shape how much a system moves its reasoning inward. An architecture that can solve multiple planning steps "in its head" in a single pass makes the model more capable but also hides those intermediate steps from safety monitors.
OpenAI's own earlier monitorability study also showed that a safer alternative exists for many use cases. A smaller, weaker base model that reasons out loud at greater length can match a huge model with a short chain of thought while staying far easier to monitor. The catch is purely economic, since longer chains of thought significantly raise compute costs in deployment.
In one encouraging result, practical deception tests in which a model was told to secretly solve side tasks or withhold capabilities on command showed that a model able to heavily manipulate its reasoning hasn't yet fooled monitors more often than an equally capable sibling model with low control over its scratchpad. OpenAI's analysis nonetheless confirms the industry's concerns. Citing Astra's scores, Google Deepmind researchers also recently warned about the gradual loss of transparent chains of thought and future architectures that reason in pure numerical codes instead of readable words. OpenAI says it urgently needs to develop new monitoring methods beyond simply reading the scratchpad to keep pace with pretraining advances.

Australia's proposed AI safety bill would force frontier model makers to open up to independent testing
Australia's government, led by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, has announced a law that would impose mandatory safety rules on frontier AI companies operating in the country for the first time. The rules target the most advanced models with the highest risk profiles and fall under the government's "AI in Australia's Interests" agenda.
A new oversight body will work alongside the Australian AI Safety Institute to enforce compliance and hand out steep penalties for violations. Companies building frontier models will have to open them up to independent audits, maintain ongoing safety checks, publish their safety frameworks, and report security incidents to the government immediately. That last requirement is partly aimed at catching early warning signs from AI agents that go off the rails.
Albanese, Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles, and ministers Tony Burke and Tim Ayres said the government is putting domestic safety guardrails in place before entering international negotiations. The goal is to protect citizens and national interests while building the kind of trust and regulatory stability that attracts investment and lets AI benefit the economy and healthcare. More details will follow once consultations wrap up.

CHICAGO—Families joined protests in seven cities nationwide on Wednesday, rallying against what they see as Google’s bid to entrench its AI models in schools, turn kids of all ages into Gemini guinea pigs, and hook them on AI.
The backlash follows a Google statement last week, confirming that there will be no way for students to use Google Search without AI. While Google claimed it was giving schools “more choice, not less”—by turning off Search, Gemini, and Gemini Notebook by default—it would not provide an option that allowed Search without AI. For students, the only way to avoid interacting with AI was to remember to add “-ai” to every query, parents worried.
In Chicago, many families showed up to protest Google, despite cold, rainy weather. Waving signs, dozens of protesters marched up to Google’s downtown office as workers seemed to be leaving for the day, shouting chants like “Hey Google, nice try, we don’t want your Gemini” and “Hey, Google, leave our kids alone!”
Called to action by a nonprofit grassroots advocacy group, the Illinois Families for Public Schools (ILFPS), some parents and students had previously won a major AI fight. In August, the group pressured Chicago Public Schools (CPS) to pull out of a Gemini pilot that would have roped in all high school students districtwide—without consulting parents. And now, ILFPS is demanding a moratorium on AI until risks to students are better understood and CPS can draft a policy to protect students from potential learning setbacks or more harmful outcomes from engaging Google’s AI bots. If the group wins, it will join cities like Los Angeles and New York City in cautiously banning AI in schools.

Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “potentially infeasible.”
Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips in order to prevent their smuggling to China. It is one of three chip-security bills under consideration for inclusion in the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, each of which is drawing renewed attention after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
When the Chip Security Act was introduced, in May 2025, lawmakers said the technology to implement it existed, something Nvidia has not publicly confirmed. In March 2026, the Semiconductor Industry Association, of which Nvidia is a member, explicitly opposed the bill and wrote that its mandates for chip tracking were “new, untested, and potentially infeasible.”
But privately, Nvidia representatives working with Foster told the lawmaker that the company could implement them.
“They never put anything in writing,” Foster says, but during technical discussions on the possibility of such safeguards, their reaction was “yeah, of course we can do this.” This private acknowledgment to Foster goes further than anything Nvidia has previously made public.
Other technology Nvidia has built for its customers suggests that the company can indeed offer accurate tracking of its chips’ locations. In December 2025, for example, it announced a new tool called Fleet Intelligence that would allow customers to monitor how its advanced chips were performing across different data center locations. In doing so, the tool could indicate which country chips were in, Nvidia confirmed to Reuters, but the company would not elaborate on whether this technology could be used to prevent smuggling.
Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment or confirmation of Foster’s characterization.
In early October, when lawmakers were reportedly increasingly concerned about Nvidia’s role in smuggling, MIT Technology Review asked the company if Fleet Intelligence could be used to prevent the practice. It declined to answer directly, instead sending a statement: “Governments and media have found insignificant diversion of controlled US products—a drop in the bucket compared to the ocean of domestic compute China already has.”
The recent fallout at Nvidia involves a number of people and companies alleged to be involved in chip smuggling. Alice Huang, with whom Jensen Huang reportedly had an affair, runs Megaspeed, a Singaporean firm now under investigation for smuggling advanced GPUs to China. A US Commerce Department inquiry into the company was reportedly halted after invention by Nvidia. Megaspeed reportedly bought chips from Supermicro, a company that packages Nvidia’s chips onto servers.

Google is continuing its elemental AI naming scheme with the new Gemini 4 Hydrogen. These names are less descriptive than the Pro/Flash monikers of earlier releases, but Hydrogen’s purpose is clear: It replaces the faster, more economical Flash models most people in Google’s ecosystem use.
With Google’s recent Argon and Carbon releases, the rollout was staged and began with cybersecurity researchers. Even when general availability began, Google restricted access to users paying for its most expensive AI subscription. The limits for Hydrogen are much more relaxed, with access beginning immediately. This model has replaced Gemini 3.8 Flash across the company’s products.
Google claims that Hydrogen represents a major improvement versus the previous Flash model. It runs in one of four thinking levels (low, medium, high, and the new xhigh), and even in high mode, it’s 2.5 times faster than Flash 3.8. Plus, it reduces “fabricated claims” by more than 5x, according to Google’s analysis. Users will also see gains in code generation, with Hydrogen more than tripling 3.8 Flash’s score in Terminal-Bench. In some cases, Hydrogen even trades blows with Argon. It managed a score of 54 in the popular Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with xhigh mode versus 50 for Argon.

Google is retiring its familiar “Flash” name and adopting periodic table elements with the global launch of Gemini 4 Hydrogen. Arriving just days after Gemini 4 Carbon, this fast everyday model is rolling out today across Google Search and the Gemini app. It brings sharper reasoning, cleaner code, and smarter web searches to everyone without requiring a paid plan.
Google called Hydrogen the biggest model upgrade ever added to Search. It now runs AI Mode by default and handles tough questions in AI Overviews, making sense of multi-part queries, typos, and conversational follow-ups. Search pages also get more visual, displaying comparison tables, custom tools, and a wider selection of source links across the web.

Inside the Gemini app’s model picker, Hydrogen replaces 3.8 Flash for everyday tasks while 3.5 Flash-Lite stays available for quick replies. Google says the new model sticks closely to formatting rules and tone instructions on the first try, pulling context from Gmail, Google Drive, and connected apps. Il flottait comme un parfum de crise autour de la table. Vendredi 6 novembre, une trentaine d’entreprises et de syndicats professionnels spécialistes de la relation commerciale franco-algérienne étaient conviés à la direction générale du Trésor, à Bercy, pour évoquer l’effondrement des échanges avec des représentants de plusieurs ministères (affaires étrangères, commerce extérieur, agriculture).
La discussion s’est résumée à un concert de doléances de la part des exportateurs français bloqués sur le marché algérien : autorisations d’importations refusées à Alger, carnets de commandes en chute libre, inquiétudes sur l’avenir de sites de production dans l’Hexagone… « Les représentants des ministères n’ont pas répondu grand-chose à nos préoccupations sinon qu’ils allaient continuer à dialoguer avec Alger, c’était assez stérile », grince un participant à la réunion.
Le mini-conclave de Bercy donne la mesure de l’impuissance de Paris face à un recul accéléré des exportations françaises en Algérie, dégât collatéral de la glaciation de la relation diplomatique depuis la reconnaissance par Emmanuel Macron, en juillet 2024, de la souveraineté marocaine sur le Sahara occidental.

Déposer son enfant à l’école le matin sans savoir s’il va être bien accueilli faute de moyens humains, c’est le quotidien de dizaines de milliers de parents en France : 39 696 élèves précisément étaient en attente d’un accompagnant d’élèves en situation de handicap (AESH) la semaine du 5 octobre, selon les chiffres communiqués au Monde par le ministère de l’éducation nationale. Cela correspond à 11 % des 362 194 élèves du primaire et du secondaire ayant une notification d’accompagnement délivrée par une commission d’accès aux droits des personnes handicapées.
Le ministère souligne que la situation s’est améliorée par rapport à la rentrée 2025, où les manquements étaient plus élevés encore, avec 48 726 enfants privés d’AESH en septembre (14 %) et 42 125 en octobre (12 %). Ces chiffres, réclamés de longue date par associations et familles, avaient alors été publiés pour la première fois par la direction générale de l’enseignement scolaire (Dgesco) dans le cadre d’une commission d’enquête menée par le député socialiste de Gironde Sébastien Saint-Pasteur. Ils révélaient aussi de très grandes disparités territoriales, comme l’avait alors détaillé Le Monde, avec plus de 30 % de demandes non satisfaites dans certains départements.
Audrey Tatry connaît bien le problème. Après avoir mené en 2022 une action en justice pour obtenir les heures d’AESH notifiées à son fils en Seine-Saint-Denis, elle a fondé Une école inclusive pour tous afin d’aider les autres parents dans cette situation. Après la publication des chiffres de la commission d’enquête, l’association avait saisi les tribunaux administratifs, en décembre 2025, pour mener une action collective contre les académies ayant les plus gros taux de carence (Aix-Marseille, Créteil, Versailles, Orléans, Nantes, Paris, Rennes, Reims, Grenoble et La Réunion).
Des territoires en grande difficulté
Dans le cadre de cette procédure, le ministère de l’éducation nationale a transmis, fin octobre, au tribunal de Paris, un mémoire de défense, accompagné de nouvelles données de la Dgesco – que Le Monde a pu consulter jeudi 12 novembre. Ces chiffres font état de 31 064 élèves en attente d’AESH au 31 décembre 2025, soit un taux de carence national de 8,7 %, en hausse par rapport au 31 décembre 2024 (27 299 élèves, soit 8,1 % de carence).

Les sénateurs ont adouci ce 12 novembre, contre l’avis du gouvernement, le relèvement du taux des cotisations à la CNRACL (Caisse nationale de retraites des agents des collectivités locales). La hausse du coût du travail dans les collectivités et les hôpitaux est limitée à 1,4 milliard d’euros dans la copie sénatoriale, au lieu de 1,8 milliard d’euros dans le texte initial.
Plan de relance agricole : « Une des thématiques majeures du compromis budgétaire », affirme Sébastien Lecornu
Dévoilé ce jeudi, le plan de relance pour l’agriculture vient compléter les mesures d’aides d’urgence de septembre destinées à compenser les pertes liées aux fortes chaleurs de cet été : « Nous avons travaillé sur deux axes majeurs : le plan d’urgence, annoncé le 4 septembre qui mobilise 1,5 milliard d’euros, et le plan de relance », commence Annie Genevard, ministre de l’Agriculture. Au total, le gouvernement apporte une réponse « à plus de deux milliards d’euros », souligne Sébastien Lecornu, avec un plan de relance sur 10 ans annoncé à « 725 millions d’euros ».
Le Premier ministre a insisté à plusieurs reprises sur le fait que la question de l’agriculture était majeure : « Personne ne doit enjamber cette question ». Il a précisé qu’elle serait « une des thématiques majeures du compromis budgétaire pour les semaines et les mois qui viennent ».
« Approfondir l’adaptation de notre agriculture au changement climatique »
Le premier axe du plan présenté ce jeudi par le gouvernement consiste à approfondir l’adaptation de l’agriculture française au changement climatique. Pour ce faire, la ministre de l’Agriculture Annie Genevard a annoncé mobiliser 100 millions d’euros « pour alimenter un guichet d’équipement qui permettra aux agriculteurs d’acheter divers outils pour protéger les animaux et les cultures face aux fortes chaleurs » comme par exemple « des citernes d’eau », de « la ventilation pour les élevages »…100 millions d’euros serviront également à couvrir à « 80 % environ 1 milliard d’euros de prêts qui permettront une adaptation durable des fermes », précise la ministre.
Le plan prévoit aussi de prolonger le Fonds hydraulique agricole en 2027, « déjà triplé cette année par le Premier ministre mais qui devait rester temporaire », souligne Annie Genevard. Cela engagera 60 millions d’euros.
Enfin, un dispositif fiscal doit être créé pour les agriculteurs qui vident leurs stocks de fourrages : si un producteur l’utilise entièrement, « sa dotation pour épargne de précaution pourra être lissée sur trois ans, ce qui évite que son résultat fiscal n’augmente », poursuit-elle.
Sortir de la dépendance aux engrais azotés
Le second axe de ce plan porte sur l’indépendance et la souveraineté agricole : « L’État mobilisera 400 millions d’euros », annonce la ministre de l’Agriculture. Dans le détail, 200 millions de fonds propres de France 2030, 150 millions de subventions France 2030, 17 millions seront transférés aux régions, 10 millions pour l’ingénierie et un surinvestissement fiscal sera mis en place.
Pour réduire la dépendance de la France aux engrais, « puisqu’on importe plus de 70% de nos engrais azotés », rappelle le ministre délégué à la Transition écologique Mathieu Lefèvre, 25 millions d’euros sont prévus pour « aider les agriculteurs à réduire leurs usages d’engrais et à se tourner vers des intrants moins polluants ». Pour la ministre de l’Agriculture, « il faut qu’on soit capable de produire nos propres engrais pour être moins dépendant ».
Pacte Genevard
Après le pacte Dutreil et le pacte Papin, deux dispositifs fiscaux qui facilitent la transmission d’entreprise, le gouvernement a décidé de décliner ce principe pour l’agriculture avec le pacte « Genevard ». « Les nouveaux agriculteurs auront un droit d’enregistrement de 0,1% au lieu de 5% en moyenne y compris et surtout pour le bâti agricole », déclare Annie Genevard. « Un gagne temps » mais aussi « monétaire » selon Mathieu Lefèvre qui explique que « les études qui conduisaient à la procédure d’enregistrement industriel s’élevaient à plusieurs milliers d’euros dans le droit existant ». Là aussi, un suramortissement fiscal entrera en vigueur pour que « le repreneur puisse moderniser son exploitation ».
« Les mesures à prendre ne peuvent pas attendre l’élection présidentielle »
La plupart de ces mesures seront inscrites au projet de loi de finances par amendements. Or, si aucun compromis n’est trouvé avec les oppositions pour voter le budget, ce dernier pourrait passer par la voie des ordonnances, une procédure qui empêche le gouvernement de modifier son texte initial pour y ajouter ces mesures en faveur des agriculteurs. Ainsi, si le budget passe par ordonnances, c’est le texte initial, sans les mesures du plan relance, qui entrera en vigueur.
Mais « les réponses » sur « comment le budget trouve son aboutissement » viendront à l’issue de l’examen par le Sénat du texte, a rétorqué le Premier ministre qui donne alors rendez-vous en « décembre ». Il a réaffirmé qu’il n’y avait « pas de schéma dans lequel il n’y a pas de budget ».
Si la question agricole sera une question de l’élection présidentielle, « les mesures à prendre ne peuvent pas attendre » : « Personne ne peut expliquer droit dans les yeux aux Françaises et aux Français, avec les taux d’intérêts qui sont les nôtres, mais aussi au monde agricole, que tout ça peut attendre un an, c’est-à-dire une saison (agricole) complète », conclut-il.

« Il est évident que là où d’autres thématiques l’année dernière », comme la suspension de la réforme des retraites, « avaient servi de discussion politique sur un compromis budgétaire, il est une évidence que la question agricole va être une des thématiques majeures du compromis budgétaire pour les semaines et les mois qui viennent », a affirmé le Premier ministre Sébastien Lecornu lors d’un point presse.
Dans le même temps, le plan de relance agricole pour 2027, déjà présenté mi-octobre, s’élèvera au final à 725 millions d’euros, a indiqué jeudi la ministre de l’Agriculture Annie Genevard, accompagnée du Premier ministre Sébastien Lecornu, lors des conclusions des Conférences de la souveraineté alimentaire lancées un an plus tôt.
Ordonnances et 49.3
« D’aucun dirait : ‘‘Le gouvernement politise la question agricole.’’ Ben non, c’est le monde réel. C’est la sécheresse et toutes les raisons qui nous ont amenés à devoir bâtir (le) plan de relance » agricole, a-t-il fait valoir. « Personne ne peut expliquer droit dans les yeux aux Françaises et aux Français, avec les taux d’intérêt qui sont les nôtres, mais aussi au monde agricole, que tout ça peut attendre un an, c’est-à-dire une saison complète », a-t-il ajouté.

Sinon, il pourrait passer par la voie des ordonnances, une procédure qui l’empêche cependant, a priori, de modifier son texte initial pour y ajouter par exemple des mesures en faveur des agriculteurs ou des lycéens.
« Responsabilité »
Balayés par l’Assemblée nationale, les textes budgétaires – projets de budgets de l’État et de la Sécurité sociale – ont repris leur parcours lundi au Sénat, hémicycle dominé par la droite qui entend faire preuve de « responsabilité » face aux finances en berne, sans savoir quel vecteur l’exécutif choisira.

Pourquoi les Français les plus aisés ont-ils payé moins d'impôt sur le revenu en 2025 que l'année précédente ?
Une étude de la Direction générale des finances publiques publiée mardi rapporte que les 10% de Français les plus fortunés ont vu leur impôt reculer en moyenne de 1,4% en 2025. Pour les 0,1% les plus aisés, cette baisse est même de 9,4%.
Le sujet est particulièrement sensible, dans un pays qui cherche à assainir ses finances. Pour les 0,1% de Français les plus aisés, l'impôt moyen sur le revenu a diminué de 9,4% en 2025, relève une étude de la Direction générale des finances publiques (DGFiP) publiée mardi 10 novembre. Les recettes de cet impôt ont quant à elles progressé de 1% au global, ce qui signifie que l'ensemble des ménages qui le paient ont contribué davantage. Ces recettes avaient déjà fortement augmenté en 2024 (+ 9,9%).
Le montant total de l'impôt net sur le revenu encaissé par l'Etat a ainsi atteint 92,6 milliards d'euros en 2025 contre 91,7 milliards en 2024, après déduction des réductions et crédits d'impôt. Mais cette hausse touche inégalement les différentes couches de la population.
Un nouvel impôt sur les hauts revenus
Les 10% de Français les plus fortunés ont ainsi vu leur impôt sur le revenu reculer en moyenne de 1,4% en 2025. La baisse est même de 5,1% pour les 1% les plus aisés du pays. Les riches parmi les riches, qui représentent 0,1% de la population, sont ceux qui ont enregistré le recul de leur impôt sur le revenu le plus important (-9,4%). Pour aider à se représenter ce que pèsent les 0,1% les plus aisés, la Direction générale des finances publiques précise que 59 000 d'entre eux ont payé plus de 100 000 euros d'impôt sur le revenu en 2025, et même plus d'un million d'euros pour 1 600 d'entre eux.
Dans un même temps, le nombre de foyers imposés, lui, est en hausse (+2,1%). Sur les 42,1 millions de foyers fiscaux qui ont déposé une déclaration de revenus pour 2025, 47,7% paient un impôt. C'est "le taux le plus important depuis 2012", relève la DGFiP.
L'explication de cette diminution de l'imposition pour les plus aisés en 2025 est à trouver du côté de la mise en place d'un nouvel impôt, la contribution différentielle sur les hauts revenus (CDHR), suppose la DGFiP dans sa note, avec beaucoup de prudence. Cet impôt, mis en place dans le budget 2025 et prolongé en 2026, assure une imposition minimum de 20% pour une personne seule dont les revenus dépassent 250 000 euros par an et 500 000 euros pour un couple. Cela a concerné environ 14 000 foyers en 2025, selon le service du ministère de l'Economie et des Finances.
Des comportements d'anticipation en 2024
Ces contribuables ont donc eu des comportements d'anticipation pour éviter de payer davantage d'impôts : déclarer davantage de revenus en 2024 en anticipant l'arrivée de la CDHR. Les revenus de capitaux mobiliers (RCM) déclarés en 2025 sont en forte baisse (-13%), après une hausse de 32% en 2024. "Cette hausse en 2024 pourrait correspondre à une anticipation de la mise en place de la CDHR", écrit ainsi le service rattaché à Bercy.
"C'est très classique comme comportement", analyse pour franceinfo Arthur Guillouzouic, économiste pour l'Institut des politiques publiques (IPP). "On sait qu'il s'agit d'assiettes fiscales qui réagissent énormément", fait-il valoir. A l'écoute des arbitrages politiques et conseillés par des spécialistes, les foyers les plus aisés anticipent les changements fiscaux pour en tirer avantage ou pour contourner toute imposition supplémentaire.
Les plus-values de cession de valeurs mobilières, qui correspondent au gain récupéré au moment de la vente, avaient également connu une forte hausse en 2024 (+16%), pour chuter de 26% en 2025. "Là aussi, la perspective de la CDHR a pu précipiter en 2024 le versement de revenus attendus normalement en 2025", explique l'étude.
Du fait de cette stratégie d'évitement de l'impôt, la contribution différentielle sur les plus hauts revenus, qui devait rapporter 1,65 milliard d'euros selon les espoirs du gouvernement, n'a rapporté que 650 millions d'euros en 2026, a fait savoir l'exécutif en janvier. Ce qui ne signifie pas pour autant que les plus aisés paient peu d'impôts. En 2025, "les 10% de foyers fiscaux disposant des revenus les plus élevés représentent près des trois quarts du total de l'impôt sur le revenu net (73%)", précisent les services de Bercy.

« Laurent Nuñez, rappelez à l’ordre vos forces de l’ordre ! » : les syndicats de journalistes ont demandé au ministre de l’intérieur, dans une lettre ouverte qui lui a été transmise lors d’une rencontre, jeudi 12 novembre, de faire cesser les violences policières contre la profession durant les manifestations.
Syndicats et directions de médias – dont l’Agence France-Presse (AFP) – ont dénoncé depuis plusieurs jours des violences des forces de l’ordre à l’encontre de journalistes, comme des coups de matraque, voire un tir de LBD, alors que ces derniers étaient identifiables avec un brassard de presse. Plusieurs plaintes pénales ont été déposées par des reporters blessés, dont une plainte collective soutenue par une intersyndicale SNJ, SNJ-CGT, CFDT-journalistes et SGJ-FO.

SOURCE 1 (Al Jazeera) :
US President Donald Trump has said he would “certainly consider” using military force against Cuba, adding that he wants to “get Cuba done” before he leaves office in 2029.
In a phone interview on Thursday with conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt, of Salem News Channel, Trump was asked whether he was considering “freeing Cuba” through a military intervention.
“I want to get Cuba done before I leave,” he said, adding that the administration was “watching it very closely”.
Trump called the island “essentially a failed … place, nation, whatever you wanna call it”.
Politico reported that it was the first time Trump had put a timeline on a possible operation.
Trump said Secretary of State Marco Rubio, whose parents are from Cuba, “would love to do it”.
“I’d love to be able to do it for the people, for the Cubans that came and were treated really badly, and they came to America,” Trump said. He added that he won the Cuban vote in Florida by a wide margin.
Pressure campaign
Trump has repeatedly threatened to topple authorities in Cuba.
On Monday, he said Cuba “will fall fairly soon” and that the US would help it “on a humanitarian basis”.
In March, he said he believed he would have “the honour of taking Cuba”, making the remarks as the island’s power grid collapsed.
Trump put Cuba under a de facto oil blockade in January, after the US seized Venezuela’s president, Nicolas Maduro, and cut off Venezuelan oil to the island.
He signed an executive order declaring Cuba an “unusual and extraordinary threat” to the US and threatened tariffs on any country that supplied it with fuel.
The blockade has caused repeated nationwide blackouts, fuel and food shortages, and a humanitarian crisis.
Cuban officials have called it “collective punishment”.
Washington has added sanctions, including on Cuba’s state oil company, President Miguel Diaz-Canel and relatives of former President Raul Castro, and announced a new round this month targeting 10 people and entities tied to the government, military and oil industry.
The US has also issued an arrest warrant for Castro. Officials from both sides have held talks on the blockade, but Cuba’s foreign minister said in June there had been “no progress”.
In March, the head of US Southern Command told senators that US troops were not rehearsing for an invasion of Cuba.
Cuban officials said the island was ready for any attack.

SOURCE 1 (Al Jazeera) :
Saudi-led coalition forces have said they intercepted suspected Houthi drones over Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh region and Eastern Province, as the UN Security Council agreed to extend sanctions on the Iran-allied group.
Major General Turki al-Maliki, the spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition, announced the interceptions of suspected Houthi drones on Thursday, in a statement carried by the Saudi Press Agency.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group had targeted oil infrastructure and military assets in the kingdom, including a pumping station on the East-West Pipeline with a drone as well as the Yanbu oil facility on the Red Sea.
Riyadh says it has rerouted about 4 million barrels of crude per day via its East-West Pipeline to Yanbu, equivalent to about 4 percent of global supply.
Saree further claimed a military cargo plane at Sharurah airport close to Yemen’s border was targeted with a drone, while a ballistic missile launched towards Khamis Mushait airbase “scored a direct hit”.
The Houthi spokesperson added that their forces had targeted the Saudi Aramco headquarters in the capital, Riyadh, but rejected as a “grave falsehood” a Saudi assertion that the group had targeted the kingdom’s Mecca region on Wednesday.
Saudi-backed coalition forces fighting on behalf of Yemen’s internationally recognised government say they continue to confront the Houthis across all frontlines, targeting leaders, vehicles, reinforcements, weapons and positions.
Yemen’s Defence Ministry, citing the Saudi-backed Presidential Leadership Council, said the battle against the Houthis was moving towards its “desired objectives”, according to Yemen’s official pro-government Saba news agency.
A meeting convened by the Defence Ministry was held in the Marib governorate to discuss the ongoing operations against the Houthis, where ways to enhance coordination and integration between various military units that are part of the Dawn of Yemen offensive were also discussed.
Security Council extends sanctions
On Thursday, the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) unanimously voted in favour of extending sanctions related to Yemen for one more year, including freezing assets and enforcing travel bans, while demanding an end to Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.
The mandate for the UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, which made the recommendations, was also extended.
UNSC members called on “all parties to refrain from escalatory actions and to resolve differences and disputes through negotiation”, while also backing the territorial integrity of both Saudi Arabia and Yemen.
“The resolution condemns the military escalation by the Houthis, their maritime and cross-border attacks against Saudi Arabia, and their threats to commercial shipping vessels,” the UNSC statement said.
The resolution emphasised that measures taken for the purpose of maintaining sanctions “shall not apply to humanitarian assistance or supplies for basic needs of civilians, without negatively affecting legitimate trade activities”.
“The council sanctions are merely a means, not an end in themselves,” said Ambassador Fu Cong, China’s envoy to the UN, who hoped that “the situation in Yemen will de-escalate as soon as possible”.
333,000 displaced
On Thursday, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said more than 333,000 people have been displaced in Yemen since the beginning of August, including more than 24,000 displaced in the past week.
Civilians “continue to pay a heavy price as violence damages health facilities, forces families from their homes, and hinders the work of humanitarians”, OCHA said.
Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia is pressing the European Union to adopt an EU Parliament resolution to designate the Ansar Allah Houthi movement as a “terrorist organisation”, according to the Reuters news agency, citing sources familiar with the drive.
But European officials told Reuters the bloc is concerned this could undermine a future peace process.
EU foreign policy spokesperson Anouar El-Anouni said the bloc was in regular contact with Riyadh on regional developments, but declined to comment on any specific discussions under way, according to Reuters.

a113.texte:
Working Paper Series 
The macroeconomic effects of 
defence spending: what impact 
beyond GDP? 
Cristina Checherita-Westphal, 
Laust L. Særkjær 
Disclaimer: This paper should not be reported as representing the views of the European Central Bank 
(ECB). The views expressed are those of the authors and do not necessarily reflect those of the ECB. 
No 3310 / November 2026 
Abstract
This paper estimates the macroeconomic effects of defence spending for a panel of up
to 27 EU member states over 1999–2025 using Panel Local Projections. We look beyond
the output multiplier that dominates the literature to trace the price implications of defence
spending and the demand-side channels through which effects operate. A key methodological
contribution is a country-specific order-date adjustment for capital expenditure, constructed
from the SIPRI Arms Transfers Database, which shifts the estimated (unitary) peak GDP
multiplier from around year one to approximately year three to four. Under this specifica-
tion, the HICP inflation response is higher and occurs earlier. Capital expenditure drives the
positive output effects, whereas personnel and intermediate consumption generate stronger
inflationary pressures per unit of fiscal impulse. Capital spending induces additional recur-
rent costs, standing at about 30 cents per euro spent over five years. Multipliers are also
found to be substantially lower, on average, in high public debt regimes.
Keywords:MilitaryExpenditure; FiscalMultiplier; LocalProjections; EuropeanUnion; Spend-
ing Composition
JEL Classification:E31, E62, H54, H56
ECB Working Paper Series No 3310
1
Non-technical summary
European governments are rapidly increasing defence expenditure. Russia’s full-scale invasion of
Ukraine in February 2022 triggered immediate budgetary responses across EU member states,
and the European Commission’sReArm Europe Planinitiative from March 2025 has elevated
national and EU-wide defence ambitions to a structural priority. Understanding the macroeco-
nomic consequences of this fiscal shift has become a priority not only for defence planners and
fiscal authorities, but also for central banks: a sustained increase in public spending at this scale
can increase inflation, shift trade balances, and interact with existing fiscal vulnerabilities in
ways that go beyond real GDP.
This paper first provides a comprehensive empirical assessment of these macroeconomic ef-
fects, particularly inflation. We use a Panel Local Projection method, tracing how each variable
of interest – real GDP, price dynamics, household consumption, net exports, and private invest-
ment – responds over a five-year horizon to an increase in defence spending, providing a richer
picture of the fiscal transmission mechanism than estimates focused solely on output. Second,
since our focus lies on European-wide effects, we use data for 27 EU member states from 1999
(and earlier) until 2025, thus drawing on more than two decades of variation in defence spending,
while also providing an up-to-date EU assessment that covers the post-2022 build-up.
Finally, a central methodological contribution of our paper is the novel correction for a
recording lag in European national accounts (the COFOG database, which classifies government
expenditure by function). Under EU accounting rules, capital spending such as major weapons
systems is recorded atdelivery, not atorder. For equipment that is often delivered several years
after it is ordered, official data show a spending increase years after the actual fiscal decision.
Using the Arms Transfers Database of the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute
(SIPRI), we construct country-specific order-date adjustments for all 27 EU member states, with
lagsrangingfromzeroyears(Malta)tofouryears(Germany, Italy, Sweden, andtheNetherlands).
Applying these adjustments shifts the estimated peak GDP response from year one to year three
to four. At the same time, the inflation effect is larger and kicks in earlier. These are important
differences for both budget planning and monetary policy assessment.
Turning to the size of estimates, a one percent of GDP increase in total defence spending
generates a GDP multiplier of approximately unity at its peak, consistent with the broader
government spending literature. Both multipliers lie below their respective peaks by the five-
ECB Working Paper Series No 3310
2
year horizon – the unadjusted settling at around 0.3, the adjusted one higher, at around 0.6. On
the price side, consumer prices (HICP) and the GDP deflator rise persistently, with the deflator
response generally larger – reflecting that defence-specific cost pressures show up directly in
government deflators, while HICP effects operate through indirect channels. In the adjusted
specification, cumulative HICP inflation reaches about 1 percentage point by year one, peaks at
about 1.4 percentage points in year three and remains at around 1.25 percentage points at the
five-year horizon. The inflation effect also holds, with a smaller magnitude, when the sample
ends in 2021, before the inflation surge.
The aggregate figures, however, conceal substantial differences across spending categories.
Capital expenditure drives the GDP effects of defence spending, generating the largest and most
persistentoutputmultiplier. Personnelcostsandintermediateconsumption, bycontrast, produce
stronger inflationary pressure per euro of fiscal impulse but more limited output effects. Capital
procurement also generatesrecurrent costs: each additional euro triggers approximately 30 cents
of additional personnel and maintenance spending over five years, implying that the true fiscal
cost of a procurement-heavy build-up substantially exceeds the initial capital appropriation.
The macroeconomic returns to defence spending also depend on fiscal space. EU member
states differ widely in their public debt positions, and countries with high(er) public debt see
substantially lower multipliers, although these estimates are imprecise.
The baseline results for total defence spending are robust to alternative lag lengths, detrend-
ing methods, and monetary policy controls, as well as to GDP weighting, leave-one-out country
exclusion, winsorising outlier observations, excluding a small residual spending category, cor-
recting for military donations to Ukraine, and measuring defence spending with the SIPRI (as
opposed to COFOG) database. Yet, substantial uncertainty surrounds the estimates, in partic-
ular the size of GDP multipliers across various periods and country samples. For the past EU
defence spending in our sample, the statistical significance tends to be stronger for higher price
effects (mostly originating from personnel spending), negative net exports, and larger recurrent
(personnel and maintenance) costs of capital procurement.
ECB Working Paper Series No 3310
3
1 Introduction
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, governments across the European
Union have announced, and in many cases implemented, substantial increases in military expen-
diture, driven both by direct security concerns and by NATO commitments to higher defence
targets. At the Hague summit in June 2025, NATO members agreed a new headline target of
5% of GDP by 2035, comprising at least 3.5% for core defence requirements and up to 1.5%
for defence- and security-related investment such as infrastructure and industrial capacity. In
parallel, the European Commission’sReArm Europe Plan, announced in March 2025, and the
subsequent activation over the period 2025-28 of the national escape clause under the reformed
EU fiscal framework have opened fiscal space for member states to act on these commitments.
Policymakers, fiscal authorities and central banks therefore need to understand the macroeco-
nomiceffectsofdefenceexpenditure, onpricesaswellasonoutput, andthedemand-sidechannels
through which they operate.
The empirical literature on defence spending multipliers has predominantly focused on the
United States, where large military buildups provide sharp and plausibly exogenous variation
in government spending (Ramey and Shapiro, 1998; Ramey, 2011; Ramey and Zubairy, 2018).
European evidence is more limited, but EU-specific estimates are emerging strongly. More fun-
damentally, the literature has focused almost exclusively on the real GDP response, leaving the
inflationary consequences of defence spending far less studied.1 This is a significant gap: from
the perspective of monetary policy, the price effects of a large and sustained fiscal expansion in
defence matter at least as much as the output effects.
The methodological backbone of the defence spending multiplier literature traces to Barro
(1981)andreceivednewimpetuswiththenarrativeidentificationapproachofRameyandShapiro
(1998), who exploit US military buildups as quasi-exogenous variation in government spending.
Ramey and Zubairy (2018) combine the local projection method of Jordà (2005) with narrative
shock identification and cumulative multiplier definitions, providing a comprehensive treatment
of US government spending multipliers, including in periods of economic slack and near the zero
lower bound. These contributions form the basis for our empirical approach.
1Price responses do feature in some recent work. For the EU27 sample, Furceri et al. (2026) find that consumer
prices rise (shown in their figure 7), and Alloza et al. (2026) report price responses alongside GDP components
for Spain, but these are typically a secondary result rather than an object of study, and we are not aware of a
systematic investigation of price effects, including by spending category.
ECB Working Paper Series No 3310
4
Fordefencespendingspecifically, thecross-countrypanelevidenceinSheremirovandSpirovska
(2022) covers a broad sample of advanced and developing economies and finds multipliers in ad-
vanced economies roughly twice those in developing ones. More generally, state dependence
in government spending multipliers has been studied by, among others, Auerbach and Gorod-
nichenko (2012), who find larger multipliers in times of economic slack, and Nickel and Tudyka
(2014), who find that high public debt attenuates them. We adapt their empirical specifications
for our debt-state analysis.
EU-specific evidence is expanding rapidly. García Serrador et al. (2025) estimate defence
spending multipliers for the EU27 using local projections, with particular attention to spending
composition and non-linearities across fiscal space and other regimes. Olejnik (2023) examines
multipliers for NATO’s eastern-flank countries over 1999–2021. For Spain, Alloza et al. (2026)
construct a comprehensive series of defence procurement contracts timed at order placement
rather than delivery, directly highlighting the timing problem we address systematically for all
EU member states through the order-date adjustment. Most recently, two IMF contributions
have analysed the topic. Furceri et al. (2026) use procurement data to estimate cumulative GDP
multipliers ranging from around 1.3 at impact to close to 2 at the two-year horizon for a panel of
EU27 countries, with multipliers larger where import intensity is low and fiscal space is ample.
The April 2026 World Economic Outlook devotes a chapter to defence spending (International
Monetary Fund, 2026), drawing on data for 164 countries since 1946. Following a peacetime
defence spending boom, real output is more than 3% higher than in periods without a boom,
with the gain materialising about two years after onset, and defence spending multipliers are close
to 1 on average. Restricting the sample to NATO members gives similar, though less precisely
estimated, multipliers, and model simulations calibrated to the planned EU build-up yield a
medium-term multiplier of about 0.8. Appendix A.1 brings these and other US, cross-country
and EU estimates together in a single figure, at short and medium horizons. They range from
about zero to above two, with a median close to one, in line with our peak estimates.
Our central contribution to this literature is methodological. Under the European System of
Accounts 2010 (ESA 2010), defence capital goods are recorded in national accounts at the time
of delivery, not at the time of order. Major weapons systems, such as aircraft, naval vessels and
armoured vehicles, are often delivered several years after they are ordered, creating a systematic
misalignment between the timing of the fiscal decision and its appearance in the data. We address
this by constructing country-specific order-date adjustments using the SIPRI Arms Transfers

Database (ATDB; Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, 2025), which records both
order and delivery dates for all international transfers of major conventional weapons. Another
contribution is to trace the macroeconomic effects of defence spending beyond output, particu-
larly on inflation, and to do so separately for capital expenditure, personnel and intermediate
consumption. We examine the demand-side channels through which these effects operate and
document the recurrent costs that capital acquisitions induce. In line with other studies, we also
estimate state-dependent multipliers, using government debt as a proxy for fiscal space.
Finally, our analysis covers up to 27 EU member states over 1999–2025, using Eurostat’s
Classification of the Functions of Government (COFOG). It thus includes the post-2022 build-
up so far, providing an up-to-date EU-wide assessment. This matters because the build-up is
fast by historical standards: in real terms, EU defence spending rose by about 10 per cent in
2024 alone, more than in any earlier year of our sample, and announced plans point to further
increases.
Our main results are as follows. Aggregate defence spending generates a cumulative GDP
multiplier of around unity at its peak, with the adjusted specification peaking later than the
unadjusted one. Price effects are positive and significant, with GDP deflator growth generally
rising more than HICP inflation. Capital expenditure is the primary source of GDP gains (but
it also generates recurrent costs); personnel and intermediate consumption generate relatively
stronger price effects per euro spent. Household consumption rises and net exports deteriorate,
particularly in reaction to personnel and intermediate consumption spending. Fiscal space con-
ditions the estimates: on average, high-debt countries see smaller output and price responses
from increased defence spending.

the construction of the order-date adjustment. Section 3 presents the empirical model. Section 4
presents the results, encompassing the baseline impulse responses, the sub-category decompo-
sition, the fiscal implications of capital procurement, and the debt-state analysis. Section 5
concludes.
